speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRESENT STOCKS IN STORAGE-REPLY TO QUESTION AS TO INCREASE IN RATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) asked me a question arising out of a press statement regarding sugar stocks in storage in Canada. According to the report to which he referred, these stocks were large, and he asked me whether in view of that situation consideration was being given to increasing the ration by approximately four pounds per person, to take up the surplus. I told him at the time I thought the situation was not such as to justify an increase in the ration. The information I have found is as follows.
While it is true that there are considerable stocks of sugar in the country at the present time, this is no indication that sugar rationing could be abandoned. In fact the world sugar situation is still quite tight, and the abandoning of sugar rationing is out of the question for some time to come.
The reason for the large stocks of sugar on hand now is that we have been receiving quite heavy deliveries of Cuban sugar against our international allocation. Under this international arrangement the actual shipments to Canada are governed by a number of factors, and we take the sugar when we are able to get it, and store it for future use.
Our allocation will allow an approximate per capita consumption of about 80 pounds this year, which is nine pounds better than last year, but still ten pounds or so below the prewar per capita consumption.

maintopic: PRESENT STOCKS IN STORAGE-REPLY TO QUESTION AS TO INCREASE IN RATION
speechtext: What is the amount of sugar in storage in Canada today? According to this statement, the storage facilities are being overtaxed because of the amount on hand. The suggestion has been made that soft drink companies, bakeries and the like be given one month's supply in advance on their quota, as is done in the United States, with a View to removing the congestion in storage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRESENT STOCKS IN STORAGE-REPLY TO QUESTION AS TO INCREASE IN RATION
speechtext: I cannot give a figure as to the amount in storage. I have not asked for that information. However I shall look into the question as to whether storage facilities are being overtaxed. The fact remains that, on balance, over the year, our allocation will not give us more than an approximate amount of 80 pounds per capita, as I said before. We take the stocks as and when we can get them.

BABIES LEAVING CANADA FOR ADOPTION IN THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
What has been the procedure whereby Canada has granted passports to babies leaving Canada for purposes of adoption in the United States?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: When a child's name is not included in the passport of its parent, an individual passport is issued to the child upon receipt of a properly executed application form "B" (for children under sixteen years of age) signed by the parent or legal guardian of the child. Proof of guardianship under provincial law is normally required. In exceptional circumstances, where such proof is not available, an application signed by a person who appears to be the legal guardian, or to have the child in lawful custody, is accepted. In all doubtful cases, the passport officer, before issuing the passport, seeks the advice of the appropriate provincial welfare authority. Passports are documents of identity which facilitate border crossings; they are not issued "for purposes of adoption".

TIMMINS (Parkdale): Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare pursuant to the press report in an Ottawa newspaper of May 13, announcing the formation of the National Cancer Institute of Canada. Will the minister inform the house whether the cancer institute is now organized, and what progress is being made, especially in regard to research?

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS IN ORGANIZATION AND RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman did give me notice of his question this morning, for which I thank him. As he and other hon. members know, my predecessor, who is now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), intimated in this house a year ago that in view of the fact that 80,000 Canadians had died from cancer during the war, and in view of the alarming state of that dreadful disease in this country as in others, he proposed taking steps to see whether some measure of coordination on the national level could not be given to deal with this tremendous problem.
I should like to take advantage of this occasion to pay a tribute to what my predecessor did in laying the groundwork for a conference which as Minister of National Health and Welfare I called on January 27-28 of this year, a conference to which were invited all the cancer control workers and cancer authorities in Canada to see whether some means could not be devised to provide for some coordinating authority with respect to this matter. As a result of that conference the Cancer Institute of Canada was set up. It is a nongovernmental, non-profit-making body. Its purpose is to deal with this problem on a national scale, not only clinically but particularly in the field of research. I do not think at this stage there is anything further I can add except to express what I know will be the hope of this house that this institute will succeed in its great endeavours.
I should add this further word. As Minister of National Health and Welfare, at the instance of the interim committee of the [DOT] institute, and as one of the trustees of the King George V cancer fund, I addressed on behalf of the institute an appeal to the trustees of the King George V cancer fund for financial assistance to enable the cancer institute to carry on for the time being. As a result of a motion made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken), the trustees of the fund have placed at the disposal of the institute on a three-year basis the sum' of $450,000 to enable the institute to carry on in the initial stages of what I trust will be a very important and fundamental work.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON COAL AND OIL SITUATION
speechtext:
I desire to make
Coal and Oil Situation

a short statement on the fuel situation. Hon. members will recall a recent statement of mine with regard to the fuel oil situation. It has now been brought to my attention that, throughout Canada, domestic coal consumers generally appear to be delaying making provision for their next winter's supply of coal. Several coal dealers have stated that coal stocks are piling up, and it will be impossible to handle the total tonnage requirements unless there is a constant and active movement of coal into domestic coal bins.
While the immediate situation would appear to be somewhat better in respect to United States coal than it was at this time last year, the situation in eastern and western Canada is somewhat worse. The eastern mines are about to reopen after a prolonged strike, and it is unlikely that any important amount of the coal lost during the shut-down can ' be recovered. In western Canada the mines are operating on a shorter work week and are already finding some difficulty in moving coal into the hands of distributors.
Last winter a combination of circumstances, particularly the bad weather, brought about a serious car shortage. This badly hampered the movement of fuel during the winter months. It is hoped that this condition will not recur, but in any event I would exhort all users of coal to exert every effort to get their supplies in during the open season.
As hon. members know, coal control was discontinued on December 31, 1946. It had been the practice during the existence of the control for the coal controller to attempt to persuade consumers to buy their coal early, and to this end he used advertising and other means. I believe this job can best be done by the coal producers and distributors now, and that the public, in its own interest, should cooperate fully to ensure that adequate supplies shall be available for next winter.
Just a word about fuel oil. I held a meeting of the principal refineries in my office this morning. I found the situation worse than I had expected. Not only will the refineries not be able to take care of new customers for fuel oil, either industrial or domestic, but it is doubtful whether they will be able to take care of the customers whom they have served in the past. The shortage is continentwide, in fact almost world wide. The difficulty is lack of transportation, lack of refining capacity and lack of oil easily accessible to markets. Therefore I should like to warn hon. members, and through them the people of this country that plans for conversion from coal to oil should be carried out only after an 
assurance has been received from a reliable source that a supply of fuel oil can be furnished.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Special War Revenue Act and to provide:
1. That the tax in respect of transportation tickets or rights of transportation
(a)	be removed in respect of transportation by vessel or aircraft extending outside the northern part of the western hemisphere, except in respect of any part of such trantsportation that is between any port or station in Canada or the United States and any other port or station in Canada or the United States; and
(b)	be extended to apply in respect of all transportation by vessel wholly within the northern part of the western hemisphere;
and that the second proviso to subsection 1 of section 32, under which section the tax is imposed, be repealed.

We were discussing,
when the house rose last night, this resolution, the effect of which would be to relieve from transportation tax purchasers of aeroplane or ocean transport going overseas from a point in Canada. Representing as I do the population of Red Lake, which is probably the largest pocket of population in the country dependent solely upon air transportation, I want to add my voice to those that were heard last night urging the Minister of Finance to eliminate the transport tax with respect to those areas where only air transportation exists. I do not think hon. members fully appreciate the great hardship that prevails in those areas because of transportation costs where transportation is a basic necessity
to the people. To go from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway to Red Lake one has to travel a distance of less than 100 miles, yet the single fare is $20, on which there would be a 15 per cent tax amounting to $3, which on the return fare of $36 amounts to $5.40. The fare cost is about four times that existing on the T.C.A. lines and about seven times the rate that those of us are accustomed to pay who ordinarily use rail transportation. You can see therefore what an imposition it is on the people there to have this 15 per cent added.
The minister said that he would consider these representations. They have been made to him for some time. The various mines in my district and in other parts of the country have been making representations to him, and I myself have spoken to him, to the minister of mines, the minister of transport and the minister of reconstruction on the subject. I do not want the Minister of Finance to think that this would be a difficult administrative problem.
The minister said that a change had been made with respect to non-scheduled air services, a change reducing the tax from 15 per cent to a tax of one cent per mile for non-scheduled air transportation, passengers only. I think that as the scheduled routes to the major mining areas are so well defined and well known, there would be no administrative difficulty in relieving them from this tax. All that would be necessary would be to provide in the bill that the department should have discretion and be able to make certain specific routes free from transport tax if it could be shown that the population depended entirely on air transportation.
I am sure the same situation that exists in my district exists in other parts of the country, particularly northern Quebec and the rapidly developing Yellowknife territory. Because the ticket costs are about seven times the rail cost, it means that anyone in those areas is paying the crown a tax seven times per mile what others pay in other parts of the country when using other means of mechanical transport.
It is not known to all members of the house that those of us who represent districts of this kind have a personal handicap that other members do not have, and that is that we are not provided with transportation passes to meet our electors in areas that can be reached, only by air transportation. I hope that at some other stage there will be an opportunity for the house to give consideration to those of us who not only pay this tax but

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After listening to the representations made by various members I said I would give further consideration to the practicability of granting a specal exemption from this tax to areas whose only effective means of transportation was by air. I have given the matter further consideration. I will not make a positive commitment at the moment. What I said last night was that before the bill was brought in I would see what could be done. I have asked the officials to work out a clause which will give this exemption but would not be subject to certain obvious abuses, which I think hon. members will appreciate. It is not free from difficulty, but I believe such a clause can be worked out, and on the assumption that it can be, it will be included in the bill. It may be necessary to come back with a supplementary resolution, but I make that statement now.

As well as those mining areas that are served by companies, there are many individual prospectors in Canada who must charter aircraft. These men are not working for large corporations that own their own aircraft; they are independent prospectors who must charter a machine to go into the north country. I feel they should be considered at the same time. They would be going into the same kind of remote areas. Will the minister make a statement with regard to another aspect of the situation, and that is taking off the tax on travel abroad. I understand there is quite a conflict going on behind the scenes between the T.C.A. and the revenue department in regard to the 'transportation that was booked by many Canadians prior to the tax coming off. Many of them feel that they have a grievance against the imposition of the tax up until the first of May. Let me give one example, which illustrates many more cases. A man books passage to Great Britain in January of this year. He happens to be in the head office the day before the tax comes off and is told by T.C.A. that the tax must be collected. That night 'the tax is off. He feels he is out $243. He is not travelling to the old country until some time towards the middle of June. He sent information today showing that in the United States this very question has arisen and the United States revenue department has issued instructions

Special War Revenue Act
that all refunds have to be made to those who have booked passages on transportation outside the country but who did not have to pay for the ticket until after the tax was removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have not paid, there is no question involved here.
But Trans-Canada Air Lines has taken the stand that according to the act they must take the tax from the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not if they have not paid for their ticket.
I know of a case which is just now being debated, where the demand was made that the fare be paid although the people are not leaving this country until the middle of June.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

They are called upon to pay the tax. The matter should be looked into and some agreement reached between the revenue department and Trans-Canada Air Lines. I realize that there must be a deadline. All those going in to book passages after May 1 know that the tax is off, but those who inadvertently or otherwise booked passage in January, February, March or April and are not leaving the country until June or July should surely not be called upon to pay a tax as heavy as the one they have to pay. I am asking the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance to look into many of these cases, and I think they will realize the injustice which many are suffering at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have had a number of representations along the line that my hon. friend has indicated. Of course, that is a problem arising every time a tax is taken off. The man who has an inventory on which the tax has been paid does not get a refund. Neither does the man who has bought some service on which the tax is paid. In this case, if he has bought his transportation and taken it up, the tax hasbeen paid, and we take the view that there is no refund available. If he has simply reserved his passage and has not paid for it, of course he gets his ticket afterwards. However, I will take note of my hon. friend's remarks.

I should like to ask this question: Has the government of Canada no policy with regard to bonuses, subventions and subsidies for air borne traffic for these outlying districts here set out in order to develop
the great natural resources up in that country? The country was undeveloped, until those were adopted for railway and canals; and now it is aircraft. For that great hinterland up north have the government no policy now, after the war, to develop air transportation? Are they leaving it for private industry to go up there and not only find the resources and develop them, but provide transportation by air unaided by subventions? There was a bonus system of subsidies and subventions for light and power and transportation, both federally and provineially. With the rich resources up in that great country where we spent so much money during the war, surely the government of Canada must have some national policy for its development and not leave it to private people. I would ask the minister to consider that matter in the recess, if this legislation cannot be amended without a ways and means measure. Now that the war has been over for two years, I think the government should 'have some policy in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is not exactly in my department. As the commiteee knows, we have appropriated substantial sums of money for building mining roads into various parts of the Northwest Territories, including Yellowknife. But in so far as it lies within the provinces, that is naturally the primary responsibility of the provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I remind hon. members that in committee we should direct our remarks to the clause under consideration. It does seem to me that the last question is not particularly in order.

I should like to add my word to what the hon. member for New Westminster has said with regard to the collection of tax on aircraft transportation overseas when the passage was not taken until after the tax was removed. I know the minister has just said that if the man did not make a deposit on his ticket he would not be subject to the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he had not bought his ticket.
But Trans-Canada Air Lines demanded that deposits be made by these people. It was a question of duress. If you wanted to get your ticket, you paid your deposit.
It was the law at that time.

I think the government is morally obligated to see that these refunds are made. I think the
Special War Revenue Act

tax under these conditions is on absolutely indefensible ground morally, although I am not going to try to argue with the Minister of Finance on legal grounds because I concede that he is my superior there.

I have a question to ask, and I will first read the clause:
That the tax in respect of transportation tickets or rights of transportation
(a) be removed in respect of transportation by vessel or aircraft extending outside of the northern part of the western hemisphere,-
It is the next part that I want to ask about.
-except in respect of any part of such transportation that is between any port or station in Canada . . .
I have been trying for some time to arrange an aeroplane trip up to Hudson bay, first stopping at the Belcher islands, then going back to the east coast of the bay to Clark islands in order to make a survey of the iron resources in that bay. There is no regular aeroplane route into that country. I shall have to engage a private plane or some private company to take me up and back. Shall I have to pay the tax on that trip?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That will be covered, if it is covered, by the further amendment that I may introduce. It has nothing to do, of course, with the resolution as it now stands, which relates simply to transatlantic and transpacific travel. I have undertaken to see if an appropriate amendment can be introduced to permit the exemption of tax on aeroplane travel into these remote areas, particularly mining areas, where there is no other readily-available means of transportation. As to what the exact terms of that amendment will be, I cannot yet say. However, I have given the undertaking that if it can be worked out I will introduce it. I cannot tell my hon. friend now whether it will cover the exact case which he has outlined. I would hope it might.
Will the minister also reconsider the transportation tax collection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is purely an administrative matter. The tax is repealed as and from May 1, 1947. It is the usual rule when a tax is removed as from a certain date, that there is no refund to one who has already paid it. We do not make refunds on inventories. We do not as a rule make refunds on taxes. It is similar to the case where a man buys something at a higher price, and the price changes the next day; he has bought a little too soon. That is the general rule in the making of 
budget changes. It is only in the most exceptional circumstances that you depart from it, and for fairly obvious reasons. We will consider the matter further, although I would not want to hold out too much hope.

I should like to ask a question with regard to draftsmanship. If the minister will look at paragraph (a) he will see that it begins by saying that the tax in respect of transportation tickets or rights of transportation "(a) be removed in respect of transportation by vessel or aircraft"; which seems to imply that the tax existed in respect to both. Then clause (b) reads: "be extended to apply in respect of all transportation by vessel". Are the words "or aircraft" left out with intent?
What does that clause actually mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a little technical, but I am advised that, in the past if you bought a one-way ticket to Europe or to Bermuda it was not taxable but if you bought a return ticket it was. Now in accordance with a similar practice adopted' in the United States with respect to this tax, if I may use the figure, we intend to put a box around the northern part of the North American continent; and tickets sold from one point within that box to another point will be subject to this tax. I think it will be made a little clearer when the legislation is actually brought down. My hon. friend will appreciate that these resolutions are drawn in rather general terms and that the statute itself will be a bit more specific.
The northern part of the North American continent; what does that mean? North of Mexico?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I answered that question
last night and said there would be a definition in the statute itself when it is brought in. I have not seen the draft of the statute and I cannot give my hon. friend that definition today, but it will be specifically defined in the terms of the statute.
Does it include Bermuda?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I am informed that it does.
And Mexico?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

1 asked the minister last evening, not out of idle curiosity, how it was that the tax on aeroplane travel was sometimes based, in the case of non-scheduled

Special War Revenue Act
flights, on a rate of one cent a mile rather than the 15 per cent rate. I wonder if he could tell me how that came about?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not too certain that
1 am quite clear on that myself; it is primarily an administrative problem, but here is the situation as I understand it. It relates largely to a private chartered plane which would be taken by an individual prospector. The charge could be on a mileage basis or at a charter rate. The plane would carry both passengers and equipment, and sometimes general freight. The department did not want to charge a tax with respect to the freight; therefore this rate of one cent per passenger mile was worked out as an alternative. That may not be too clear but I am afraid it is the best I can give my hon. friend at the moment. If he would like a further explanation I would be happy to refer him to the officials of the department.

I am more interested in the general principle behind this matter than in the actual tax of one cent a mile on non-scheduled flights. I find that in a number of cases we pass taxation statutes here, framing them as we think they were intended to be framed by parliament. By the time they are operated upon in the national revenue department however, they bear little resemblance to the original. 1 want to know just how it comes about that when we pass a law imposing a tax of 15 per cent on aeroplane travel the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance sees fit to change the basis of the tax.

Will the minister give
me some information about this tax on passengers in chartered planes? When a plane is chartered to carry both passengers and goods, is the tax applied to both passengers and goods, or to the passengers only?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just the passengers.

I think it is a commendable thing, of course, when we are asked to pass anything that removes some tax and :herefore I do not see how I can oppose this particular item. But personally I am opposed to any tax on railway and steamship travel, for the reason that the tax is imposed upon a service which is given. I can quite understand when the government has to obtain revenue, as it does under the system under which we are now operating, how they have to look around for sources of taxation. I can quite understand how they could reasonably tax chewing gum and lipstick and a few other things of that kind. But that is something people buy, something they have, something they use and wear out or keep as long
as they wish. Here is a tax on a service which is given. People do not carry it home with them; it is a service they are compelled to have. I can understand-perhaps I would not know how to designate it-how a tax might reasonably be imposed upon pleasure travel, but you see we are so constituted that if we want to go somewhere we cannot get there without taking our bodies along with us. Therefore we need a little transportation. This is a service given to us, and we are taxed upon a very necessary service. I am opposed to that because, as the government looks for new sources of revenue, the first thing we know we are going to be taxed upon other types of services.

Don't give them new
ideas.

Perhaps when I remove
my baggage to the train, or when I take a taxicab somewhere, I will find myself paying a tax. I do not suppose they would be so mean, shall I say, as to tax doctors' bills, but a doctor renders a necessary service, and the first thing we know the government is going to say, "We have taxed this service and that service; perhaps we can tax doctors' bills." All sorts of services are being taxed. I think we have to cut this thing off somewhere and cut it off as short as we can. I do not think any government has a right to tax such things as necessary services that are given.

I want to ask just one question before this item carries. The air transport board have licensed a number of carriers for certain routes; I am thinking of several emanating from Toronto, which are occasional carriers. During part of the season they run fairly regularly, and in the winter perhaps they do not run at all. I understand that under the regulations these carriers would be taxed at the rate of one cent per passenger mile, though they are definitely licensed to operate from certain points to certain districts. I am thinking of the service from Toronto to Muskoka and Toronto to Lake of Bays, and further north. On the other hand mining operations, such as the service from Kenora to Favourable Lake, which has a definite rate but no definite schedule, because it is a definite prescribed trip operated by Canadian Pacific Air Lines would be taxable under the 15 per cent rate, whereas the other services would be taxed only at the rate of one cent per passenger mile. I point out to the minister that in the one case the tax is extremely unfair, while in the other it has to do with
Special War Revenue Act

what is more or less a pleasure type of travel which probably should stand the extra impost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, if I am able to follow out what I hope I may be able to do-that is, eliminate this tax where the flight would be made to a certain area where there is no other means of transportation-that would eliminate the 15 per cent tax and the cent tax as well. It is explained that that cent tax is in lieu of the 15 per cent tax, and applies only, in addition to the matter of the unscheduled flight, to where the plane is carrying both passengers and freight. If the plane were carrying passengers, only 15 per cent would apply to the price of the flight. But it is to get away from charging this tax on the freight that this was worked out, after consultation with the air transport companies. They advised the department that that was equitable, and worked out, as closely as could be arrived at, at the 15 per cent rate on the passenger part of the load.

2. That the tax on syrups enumerated in customs tariff items >139 (except glucose and grape sugar) and 140 (except molasses) be reduced from two cents per pound to one cent per pound.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I might give an explanation. The purpose of this amendment is to remove present anomalies in the sugar tax structure. Prior to the war, table syrups and corn syrup sold for domestic use were taxable at the same rate as granulated sugar. During war time, for price ceiling reasons, the tax on sugar was reduced from two cents a pound to one cent a pound, although the tax on table syrups and corn syrup was left at two cents a pound. The amendment at present proposed would bring the tax on syrups into line with the tax on sugar of one cent per pound. Revenue from the sugar tax in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947, was about $11,300,000.
This lowers the rate to one cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

This resolution involves an amendment to section 80 of the Special War Revenue Act. Under that section we deal with the tax on soft drinks. I should like to make a few submissions to the minister today in respect to that tax.
If he will remember, we had a spirited discussion last session; at that time he made some concessions to the tea and coffee drinkers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The committee is now considering resolution No. 2, with respect to syrups. I do not think at this

time a discussion on soft drinks should be allowed. I should think when second reading of the bill is before the house the discussion might be in order; but it is not related to this resolution.

The minister did not raise any objection-and rightly so, I suggest. I submit that the resolution involves a change in section 80 of the Special War Revenue Act, because it concerns a schedule under that section. In that same schedule we find a portion of the tax on soft drinks. Furthermore this item has to do directly with the same group of taxes. The same commodity, sugar, is required for the manufacture of soft drinks. So that in two ways I say it is relevant to have the discussion now.
I submit, sir, that you are unduly zealous in raising the point at this time. Certainly if I am in order in discussing the matter on the bill, I am equally in order in discussing it on this resolution, and I submit I should not be ruled out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I might add a word. I agree with the view taken by the chairman, that my hon. friend is not strictly in order when he proposes to discuss the soft drinks tax on this resolution. He would be completely in order if he were to make a speech on second reading of the bill. I took the same stand last night in connection with the hon. member for Peterborough West.
The tax on soft drinks comes in here only because it is in the schedule referred to in section 80, along with a great many other commodities. This is a very narrow change in the act, and relates solely to bringing into line the tax on table syrup and corn syrup with the changed tax on sugar.
If we were to allow a discussion on this very interesting topic of soft drinks in the committee stage on this resolution, I believe we would have to allow the discussion to take place in detail, and to answer questions in detail in respect of all the other commodities taxed (under the schedule. I submit that would be going a long way. My hon. friend will have the fullest opportunity of placing his views on the question of soft drinks before the house when the bill is introduced, one sec-

Special War Revenue Act
tion of which will relate to this resolution. I do suggest, however, that he is out of order now.
On the minister's own argument I am in order, because he has said I can discuss it on a section of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I said it could be discussed on second reading.
Or on second reading. If I can discuss it on a section of the bill, then I can discuss it here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My answer is that the hon. member cannot discuss it on a section of the bill.

I do not want to carry my submission to the extent of having to appeal from the Chairman's ruling. I understand, sir, you have not made a ruling yet, in any event. But I submit I am in order, bearing in mind the two points I have mentioned. Certainly I am in order on the ground that sugar is required in the production of soft drinks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And a great many other things are required, too.
This is part of the tax on sugar. Now, the minister may not like to have this subject discussed; I do not doubt that he is trying-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nonsense. I can discuss soft drinks as well as my hon. friend. I have had as many letters as he has.
Perhaps that is why he is trying to put off the discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My reason is that I am endeavouring to cooperate in completing the proceedings of the house, in order and within a reasonable time. If we debate all those resolutions in the schedule in respect of which sugar ia a raw material, then surely the field is wide open. My hon. friend or any other member in the committee may make any speech he likes on second reading of the bill to amend the Special War Revenue Act. He can talk about soft drinks, or about the candy tax or any of the other taxes imposed under that act. But when we are trying to have passed through committee a resolution which authorizes the introduction of a bill to make certain specific amendments, then it seems to me it is out of order to throw the door wide open and to discuss any commodity tax imposed under the provisions of the Special War Revenue Act. That is what my hon. friend is suggesting.
The minister does not want to have the session delayed by the opposition asking questions, and I can quite understand why.
He did not say that.

We can understand why he takes that position. I would do the same thing if I were over there. But I submit that if we are to be bound down when the house is in committee, in a manner such as has been suggested by the minister, we would have imposed upon us an entirely unwarranted restriction of our rights as members of the house.
It will be noticed that the minister did not raise this point of order. He was perfectly willing to have the discussion go on. The chairman was the culprit. I suggest that I be allowed to proceed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did raise the point of order, because I try to keep discussion in committee within the bounds of the rules. It occurs to me, with considerable force, that there are about 79 other items in the schedule.
If you are going to make a ruling, Mr. Chairman, will you allow me to say one word further?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I conclude my statement? I will give the hon. member opportunity to make his remarks before I give my ruling. As the minister has stated, there are eighty items in the schedule, and if we allow a discussion at this time on soft drinks there is no reason why we should not allow a discussion on any of the other seventy-nine items. But I do not think that would be the wish of the committee. After hearing everything that has been said so far I still feel that the discussion on soft drinks would not be in order at this time, but as I said, I shall be glad to hear from the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not base my remarks on technical rules of order, but I think the discussion should be allowed as a matter of convenience and common sense. Under all the circumstances, therefore, the government has decided to rescind order in council P.C. 1502 and this decision has been carried out. In lieu thereof, I am proposing to amend section 5 (1) (v) of the Income War Tax Act in such a way as to provide that the period to be determined by the governor in council for the purposes of the subsection shall be a twelve months' period to be named by the governor in council ending not later than December 31, 1950. The bill which will be introduced when the house has dealt with all these resolutions will contain this amendment.
It will be noted that the governor in council will have a certain measure of discretion as to the choice of the period, but he cannot delay his decision indefinitely; under no circumstances can he name a period later than the year 1950. The end of the twelve months' period therefore is bound to come within about five years after the end of the war. This, it seems to us, is the most reasonable solution of what has been a rather difficult problem. It will enable us to avoid aggravating still further the shortage of material and labour that exists at the present time. It will make it possible to postpone the special inducement to expanded maintenance work until some time when conditions are at least "less tight" than at present and perhaps to a time when it may be desirable to have the increased employment which the special provision should encourage. It will, we believe, make it possible for taxpayers to do some advance planning and to defer certain less urgent types of work to be carried out during the twelve months' period to be named at a later day.

I have a suggestion to offer to get rid of the income tax altogether. Some articles have been published in a Montreal daily explaining the whole thing, and I shall try to summarize it as briefly as possible. The data is from the "Canada Year Book, 1945," because I received the 1946 issue too late to deal with it.
In 1944 the total income for national revenue was 89,200,000,000, earned by 5,000,000 people. One-half of them, or 2,450,000, earned revenue amounting to $4,767,000,000, or approximately one-half of the national revenue. The income tax amounted to $682,000,000, or fourteen per cent of the total yearly income of one-half of the working or earning population. That proportion of the earnings of the people came from the best class of people, namely the middle class and the poor.
To refer again to the "Canada Year Book, 1945," the government states therein that the banks submit regularly true accounts of every banking transaction they handle. According to these statements to the government, the banks during 1944 cashed cheques amounting to $60,000,000,000 and passed over counter currency involving $25,000,000,000. So it appears that banking operations in Canada attained $85,000,000,000 in 1944.
The banks are compelled to make a monthly report to the government. Why then should not the government avail itself of this opportunity to impose on the banks the obligation of deducting a fraction of their transactions, perhaps to the extent of one per cent. Taking as a basis the last statement of the banks, the state could derive from that tax $850,000,000. By the same process, every individual would recover the right to save or spend or invest his money as he wishes, among other things leaving him free to better his own position in life and to contribute more liberally to the social welfare and care of the needy.
Moreover this form of taxation would assess the taxes more equitably on the whole of the population fit to work, without setting a heavier ransom. Each individual would pay according to his means and according to the proportion of his business transactions.
The forms which the income taxpayers must fill out are real Chinese puzzles, and the law itself is so entangled that a great number of people are unable to get through its many riddles without help; while on the other hand the proposed new principle of taxation, to be levied as a duty on banking operations, presents no complications whatever, and is most easy to understand. In fact the main criticism that has been made by the press was that it was too simple to be adopted. If it were more complicated there would be a better chance of having it adopted. But under this new principle of taxation nobody would have to rack his brain any more or

Income MTar Tax Act
to employ accountants to prepare the yearly report which would be supplied to the state by the banks in the course of their routine business, for they are already compelled to make a daily statement on the cheques they handle, and thus time and worry would be saved to the people.
The monetary system of the country, as we know, is under the exclusive control of the federal government.
The proceeds of the special tax we propose would depend upon the commercial activities of the taxpayers and on the amount of money put in circulation therefrom. It is a logical result that the flow of money should increase in proportion to the commercial activities of the country. From 1935 to 1944, the approximate amount of the national revenue and the total of the rolling funds doubled in 1941 and trebled in 1944 from their levels of 1935.
The figures in connection with the national revenue are calculated only by approximation, but banking statements on fluctuation of credits reflect with much more accuracy the progress of our commercial situation.
These bank reports indicate that our economic progression is rapid and constantly moving forward. These healthy conditions should be a source of increasing revenue for the state without having recourse to an increase in the rate of the tax.
Now let us consider how notoriously inefficient is the collection of the income tax. In order to collect it, the government must stand as the censor of the expenditures made by all the taxpayers, of their family budgets, of their donations to charity and, in addition, it must reckon on the accuracy and the reliability of each individual making a report.
With the system we propose, which is in reality a duty on every cheque passed through a bank, all those hindrances should be nonexistent. At the same time, it should yield to the state, as we have already shown, $850 million, if we take as a basis the 1944 report of $85 billion of bank clearings at the rate of one per cent.
Once more we insist on the fact that this indirect tax would be much fairer than income tax, because it would be paid by all, not by only one-half of the people. It would also be more logical, because the tax would be proportionate to the amount of the cheque. For instance, the beneficiary of a cheque would pay $1 on a cheque of $i()0; $10 on $1,000; $100 on $10,000, and so on. In short, the tax on bank credits would be spread over all the population, and everyone without exception would pay it proportionally to his commercial endeavours.

If the payment of the income tax were shared by all the ratepayers on this same basis the average cost would amount to six per cent instead of being, as it stands, fourteen per cent on the income of those who have paid their fiscal dues. This is figured on the amount of the income tax paid in 1944 and with reference to the total of the national revenue, only one half of the debtors having paid the income tax.
For the purpose of showing the mechanism of the proposed tax and making its working clear to everybody, we take as an example the case of a merchant who buys from a manufacturer some articles for an amount of $10,000. The manufacturer, creditor of the merchant, cashes the cheque he received in payment; the bank retains $100 on it as tax at the rate of one per cent. To help him sell his goods, the merchant employs clerks, to whom he pays $3,000 as their salary. These clerks, creditors of the merchant, deposit their cheques at the bank and are credited with the amount less the tax, namely $30, which is retained by the bank. Now the sale of the merchandise has yielded $16,000, which represents a profit of $3,000 on the original purchase price and includes the salaries of the clerks. So the merchant deposits $16,000 at the bank, and the bank withholds one per cent, which is $160.
In all these banking operations, the following taxes would have been paid on commercial transactions amounting to $29,000:
By the producer	 $100
By the clerks	 30
By the merchant	 160
Tax on the bank credits	 $290
Following this operation, the capital of the merchant has been increased by $3,000 less $160, making a net profit of $2,840; the tax taking only 5-3 per cent of the merchant's profit. This rate cannot fail to be maintained, with the increasing amount of business, whereas, with the present system of the income tax, the contrary happens.
If the business done by a merchant continues at the same rate every month, as shown here, we have only to multiply by twelve to obtain the total amount of the business done during one year and the total of taxes paid:
By the producer on $120,000	 $1,200
By the clerks on $36,000	 360
By the merchant on $192,000	 1,920
Taxes on bank credits	 $3,480
According to the actual rate of the income tax, the merchant who realizes an annual profit of $3,000 pays $506 if he is unmarried,

and $278 if he is married with two children. If he makes a monthly profit of $3,000, or twelve times more, he pays $16,450 in the first case, and $15,670 in the second; whereas, if the proposed tax were in force, this merchant would pay only $160 in the first case and, in the second, $1,920.
We want to relieve the salaried men who are paying, at the present time, the greater part of the income tax. The method of taxation we are explaining does not apply exclusively to income, but extends to all banking transactions. Those who carry on the more numerous and more important commercial enterprises should pay proportionally to their financial activities, which is only right.
It is easy to figure that, under the new mode of taxation we are proposing, the tax affecting revenue would be much lower and more equitable than it is at present; because each creditor, or beneficiary of a cheque, would be charged a tax of only one per cent on each payment made to him by a debtor. The fact is that banking debits represent the total amount of negotiated cheques each day at the banks.
As we have already said, if this new method of taxation were adopted, private individuals and corporations, except banks, would not have to produce income tax returns. The banks would take care of that themselves by the simple process of retaining one per cent on every cheque deposited or cashed in future. They would thus become the government's agents for the collection of duties on the banking credits of the depositors. These would know immediately and exactly what they should have to pay. The paramount importance which the bank account occupies in our economic life is pointed out, each year, in the "Canada Year Book," published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In the latest issue, that of 1945, we find on page 1051 the following statement about the payment of accounts by cheques:
In every progressive industrial community currency represents only the petty cash of commerce. The greatest part of all commercial exchanges, especially when large deals are involved, is done through the medium of banks. About six per cent only of all financial transactions of the country, it appears, are done by means of currency; the other 94 per cent are negotiated by cheques. Thus, if we are able to ascertain the global sum of all cheques paid by the banks, or charged to the accounts of their clients, we would possess a nearly complete estimate of the volume of business carried out, therefore an accurate knowledge of the commercial activities of the country.
Since 1924. the bankers' association has consented to give out, in a monthly report, the figures on the amount of business passing through the clearing houses in the most important centres of the country.
Based on these statements, the federal office of statistics publishes a monthly and yearly return of these figures comprising all cheques charged by the banks to the account of their clients. Moreover, a report on the credit and debit balances of the banks is made over by the manager of the clearing house to the Bank of Canada, the latter obtaining from every bank, through telephone or telegraph, a confirmation of the accuracy of the report. Then, the Bank of Canada enters daily this balance sheet on the account of each bank on the debit or credit side, whatever may be the case. This is how nearly all banking transactions of the country are compiled daily at Ottawa.
It is easy to see that the federal government has already in hand the necessary- organism to collect the proposed tax on banking credits. If parliament should see its way to replace the income tax by this new tax, the simplicity and flexibility of which are striking, it could authorize the government to fix its rate which should never exceed the maximum established by law. By its adoption, the government would get rid of its present obligation of auditing the accounts of each taxpayer. What a relief that would be for them.
Another point in favour of the proposed tax is that it would put an end to numerous anomalies which are contrary to common sense
Income War Tax Act

and fairness. For instance, a large number of people who make big profits by the sale or the exchange of real estate property, by the promotion of companies, by the sale of corporation shares, et cetera, do not pay any taxes on these commercial operations. Under the new plan, that kind of business activity would be automatically taxed by one per cent. Speculation on the fall of stock and any business negotiated at a loss should also re taxed.
Now we come to the fact ti. jt ninety-four per cent of all commercial deals are made by cheques, and six per cent, only by currency. So the practice which is already in current use could be rendered compulsory by law. Everyone would be ordered to deposit into chartered banks all the currency he possesses. This rule would be made effective by replacing all bank notes in circulation by a new issue completely different from the one actually in use. This new' currency would become the only legal one in Canada. New issues of currency, at regular intervals, would force gvery ratepayer to apply periodically at the banks to exchange their currency for tha new one. Without a special permit the banks would not be allowed to grant more currency than S100 at one time to any one person. Every person who would possess more money than authorized by regulations would be under the obligation to account for it, the over-plus being subject to confiscation.
In order to facilitate their clients in carrying on their daily business, the banks would deliver to them, on demand, a book of certified cheques of small denominations, that is, $1, $5, $10 and $20, similar to travellers cheques. These cheques would bear the signature of the bank and that of the client and would be perforated so that the value could not be altered. Whenever the customer wished to use them he would countersign them, enter the amount and the name of the beneficiary. On presentation of the cheque by the beneficiary the bank would deduct one per cent for the tax. If the beneficiary transferred the cheque to a third party the latter would have to endorse it, and then the bank would deduct two per cent instead of one and so on increasingly at one per cent each time for each additional endorser.
We hear very often that it is the rich man who pays the income tax. It is easy to prove this assertion as false and contrary to the existing facts. The statistics show that on
2,450,000	individuals who paid income tax in 1944, the latest year for which we have official figures, 2,270,000 taxpayers whose taxable income amounted to less than $2,000 contributed to the tax. So we cannot do [Mr. Pouliot.}
otherwise than come to the conclusion that this tax hits the bulk of the population, by striking at the middle class and the poor.
Here is a list of those with earnings of less than $3,000 a year. A summary outlined in regard to the 2,270,000 persons who earned less than $3,000 and were taxed reads as follows; in 1944, 385,000; in 1945, 425,300 earning less than $1,000; in 1944, 1,290,000, and in 1945, 1,250,000 earning from $1,000 to $2,000; in 1944, 695,00 and in 1945, 478,200 earning from $2,000 to $3,000. In order to complete the table we must add that 80,000 individuals having an income from $3,000 to $4,000 and
35.000	with an income of from $4,000 to $5,000 paid the tax. Throughout the country, of a total of 2,450,000 persons who paid income tax there were only 65,000 with a taxable income of over $5,000. These were the figures for 1944.
In 1945 there were 144,000, instead of
115.000	in 1944, with earnings of from $3,000 to $5,000 who paid the tax. In 1945 there was a surplus of 500 earning over $5,000 who paid the tax. Consequently we are convinced that in suggesting to suppress the income tax we are defending the cause of the middle class as well as that of the poor.
We have heard friends confiding that they were unable to give to a sick wife or sick children the medical care they should have received precisely on account of their lack of money, a relatively considerable part of their earnings being withheld by their employer for the income tax. It is no secret that numerous heads of families are compelled to withdraw from schools their most promising children because, after having discharged their income tax dues, they are unable to save anything. So, when at the age of sixteen the child loses his right to family allowances the father is not left with enough money to keep him in school.
The thriftiness of the Canadian population is to be greatly admired, and it is deplorable that it has become nearly impossible for a man who is the father of a large family, and also for the unmarried man who has dependents, to provide for their old age. Especially since the last war, this fact is more obvious on account of the high rate of taxation. How many of our fellow citizens do we see working late at night so as to be able to pay their insurance premiums? More often than not, they must work on the sly, because the income tax act-does not always allow them to keep for themselves any compensation for overtime work.
The income tax is a source of restlessness and worry for those who, despite the hardships they have to suffer, find it a difficult matter to make both ends meet. That form of

Income War Tax Act
taxation, even perverts our population by inciting to heedlessness and laziness. We hear people saying, "What good is there to work harder if we get in return no benefit whatever from our overtime work?"
The income tax is also an indirect cause of labour strikes because, if the taxpayer were not deprived of that part of his pay, he would otherwise be nearly always satisfied by getting a fuller amount of his earnings.
During the war, when parliament was voting blindly billions over billions of dollars, we could not help thinking of the results on our economic system in the years to come.
We had many occasions to discuss the matter with that great Canadian, the lamented Mr. Cardin, for whom we had a profound esteem; and while we were exchanging together our views, which were rather gloomy, on our future, we could listen to the claim of a certain class of optimists insisting that we were amidst a period of transition, and that everything would be rosy and pink-coloured after the war. The war is over, and not even a tinge of pink is yet visible on the farthest distant horizon.
Well, after having heard the sighs of despondency, the demands, the complaints, soaring up from all classes of society, we have consulted leading businessmen and bankers; and we have tried to find the best means to lessen the burden which weighs on the people.
If this plan of a tax of one per cent on all cheques were adopted, the 385,000 taxpayers whose income is less than $1,000 would pay only $5,290,000 instead of $19,700,000 in taxes; the 1,290,000 having an income of from $1,000 to $2,000 would pay $19,620,000 instead of $146 million; and the 695,000 in the $2,000 to $3,000 bracket, $14,040,000 instead of $158,400,000.
No error is possible. The rate could be no more than one per cent of the total of banking credits amounting approximately to $85 billion. It would bring $850 million to the public treasury. Every individual would pay according to the number and the importance of his commercial dealings, and nobody would have to submit any form of declaration.
This tax would not in any way affect deposits at present in the banks, but would be applied in the future on cheques negotiated through the banks. Mathematically, it would apply on all the commercial activities of the country: profits on capital, exchange, rolling capital, profits, salary; contrary to the present tax which affects only new capital and earn-'ings.
We have submitted only the broad lines of our proposal. It was impossible to do otherwise in the restricted frame of this sketch, but a careful study, with a view to ironing out
possible objections relating to particular conditions, could easily render this proposed tax the most efficacious and reasonable, and certainly the most equitable of our fiscal
measures.
I thank you, sir, and my colleagues as well for having paid so much attention while I was explaining the plan in as concise a manner as possible. People are under the impression that it is only the rich who pay income tax, but it is not so, and one effect of such taxation is not to take from a man what he can pay but to get from him all that can possibly come out of his pocket. Of course it is hard. It is pretty difficult. I will not insist on what happened during the war, when I was one of those who opposed reckless expenditures, but now we must consider the present as it is, and it is the duty of every member of parliament to offer suggestions.
I do not suggest that I am infallible; I do not contend that this proposal is a perfect cure. It is. however, a suggestion. What it is worth I cannot say, but I have offered the proposal in complete earnestness in a desire to relieve the people of the burden that weighs so heavily upon their shoulders, and I hope the minister will consider it in due course. I do not expect that it will be done this year. It may take years to do it; but the later it is done, the worse. Something should be done right away.
Everyone must use his own imagination in making suggestions. Are we to stay in the mud of the ditch without thinking of bringing the car on to the road of prosperity? I hope that what is proposed will come in due course. I thank the committee again.

He pictured to us a situation which I do not think exists, and which, I am sure, those who have had experience with the various local income tax offices of the Department of National Revenue find does not exist; that is, that the backlog would be reduced, and this advisory board would begin work at an early day. At that time I suggested to the minister that if conditions continued as they were then and as they had existed for some time, this board would not go to work before about 1949. I estimated that the present backlog had been running about three years in arrears, so it could hardly be expected that the board would have any work to do before 1949. The backlog still continues; and I think the committee would be interested to know' when this board is going to go to work.
As far as the revision of the act is concerned, I renew to the minister a suggestion I made last year. It was not a novel suggestion then; I am sure it has been made often in this house, and it was repeated last night by the hon. member for Grey North in an eloquent and forceful manner. I refer
{Mr. Fleming.]
to the title of the act. Surely, if the time has come-and I put this position before the committee because I am quite sure hon. members will appreciate the reasonableness of it-when the fiction attached to the title of the Special War Revenue Act should be removed, equally the time must have come to remove the fiction from the title of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has come. We are taking "war" out of this act, too.

I am sure that announcement will be received by the committee with the utmost satisfaction.
In conclusion, I should like to invite the minister, if he will be so good, to make a statement on the matter of deductions. The first resolution before us, while it establishes the new scale of taxes, does so by way of fixing the scale of deductions. When deductions at the source with respect to salaries and wages were first decided upon, the house will recall that ninety per cent was the percentage of deduction, on the theory that ten per cent was the percentage allowed to any person in respect to charitable donations, so it was felt that would be a reasonable amount. The idea of deductions at the source was sound, since it enabled, people to pay as they went along, and to avoid being faced at some later day with an accrued liability of substantial proportions which they might find it difficult to pay. That idea was sound. In a later amendment. I think three years ago, the percentage of deduction was increased to ninety-five per cent. The reason given at the time, if I remember correctly, was that ninety-five per cent was thought to be closer to the amount of actual liability, according to the experience of the department in connection with the returns filed in the following spring of each year.
In view of the time that has elapsed since then, I think the house should be given a report by the minister on the way in which the present percentage of deduction is working out with reference to tax liability; because, with what I think is a trend toward increased charitable givings, it may be-I can only conjecture this in the absence of any report, of an official nature-that perhaps ninety per cent is as close to the actual amount as ninety-five per cent. In any event, if there is very little to choose I submit that the taxpayer should be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, when the margin is so narrow. I say that particularly because of the delay in repayment to taxpayers from whom more has been deducted than is required to meet their tax liability. As long as we are to have a backlog of work in the department which delays the payment of

Income TFar Tax Act
refunds for a year, two years or three years, then I say it is not fair to require the deduction of more than is reasonably necessary to meet the tax liability.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I had better answer the two or three points raised by my hon. friend, and I should deal first wTith the question of the preparation of the new act. I am not prepared to concede that there has been any undue delay in the preparation of that revised act. It has been really a tremendous task;
I do not think that word is too strong to use. Officials of the. Department of National Revenue, the Department of Justice and the Department of Finance have been working long hours during the last seven or eight months to prepare this revised text; and I am satisfied that even after it is brought into the house and, has had the consideration of hon. members, when it becomes available for consideration by such groups as the association of chartered accountants and others who are specialists in this field, other desirable changes will be suggested. As I say, it is an important matter; but in the order of priority I think there are other matters which have been engaging the attention of the officials I referred to and of my predecessor during the last, year or two, and which are of higher priority. For that reason I am not prepared to concede that there has been any undue delay; nor am I prepared to concede that our present income tax law is anything nearly as defective as some people w'ould make it out to be. It is not perfect, certainly, but over the course of years I have had a good deal of experience in the practical application of that law, and I make the assertion with confidence that it is not nearly as imperfect, not nearly as obscure as some people would pretend it to be. Anyone who is familiar with the income tax laws of other jurisdictions, and particularly that of the United States, will find that our law has a good, deal to commend it, even in its present form.
However, it is my intention to bring in this bill within the next couple of weeks, if possible, or probably in three weeks, and at that time the house will have an opportunity to consider it. As I said in my budget speech, I think they will find that it will be desirable to discuss it here for a time, and then to hold it over, and take it up early in the next session. But that is a matter which will rest with the house.
Then, as to the matter of the appeal board and the advisory board; in view of the fact that I think it will be possible to eliminate a very large number of these discretionary powers it may not be necessary to set up an advisory board as such. We shall be able
to do away with that. We shall need the appeal board which, in effect, is a type of court, and will be between the minister and the exchequer court. That we propose to set up, and I hope it will be possible to set it up within the next few months.
The last point mentioned by the hon. member had reference to deductions. The basis followed now is that of a ninety-five per cent deduction. The experience we have had so far is perhaps not sufficient to enable us to form a final opinion. There have been a substantial number of refunds on the ninety-five per cent deduction. On the other hand, the objection to underdeduction and having to pay later, is equally strong, where the majority of w'age and salary earners believe that their full income tax has been paid, by deduction at the source.
However I am glad to have the point raised, and I can assure the hon. member we are looking into it closely. If it is found that the ninety-five per cent deduction results in an excessive number of refund payments, then I agree it should be lowered to ninety per cent.

Do I understand that
two bills will be introduced, one of which will deal with the amendments in the thirteen resolutions and, when that is disposed of, an entirely different bill is t.o be introduced which will contain the new act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That is correct. I propose

Then, in addition, I shall introduce a complete new income tax bill, which w'ill cover the whole field, and which will contain a number of provisions that are completely newT, so far as the existing act is concerned. Some of those changes will involve important questions of policy which the house will have an opportunity to debate, and which, I hope, will be carefully studied by people throughout the country, including chartered accountants and lawyers who are specialists in these matters, and also by taxpayers generally. I listened with great interest to what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton. Among other things he mentioned assessments. First, I should like to make an appeal to the Minister of National Revenue. I know something about conditions which pertain in the income tax office in Toronto. They are very much crowded at

that point, and the conditions under which they have to work are bad for their health and for the efficiency of the office. I make the plea to the Minister of National Revenue that he do something about this condition, with a view to getting better quarters for them to work in, if it is possible to do so. I now wish to make a plea on behalf of married women who are working. The point is that a married woman is today allowed to earn only $250, without having an additional deduction made. In these days when drives are being made for nurses and schoolteachers, and for women to work in laundries, I think some change should be made in this law. These are places where, as a rule, single women do not work. There are many places where married women can work to advantage, and be most useful.
I said something about this in my speech on the budget. The plea I make is for the married women to be permitted to make a little more money, without having her husband penalized. At the present time all she can work is about 400 or 500 hours a year. As the children get older, the mothers can go out and do useful work; and want to. The children do not require so much attention, but they require more food, and more money is required to defray the expenses in connection with them-clothes and a few chocolate bars, and pop.
Is it not fair not to allow these married women to make a little more money so that they can help out their husbands, especially in view of the high cost of living prevailing today? The children need better food and better diet and, as I have said, these things must be obtained, despite the higher prices which prevail.
Why penalize a married woman who is in a position to work today? At this time $250 is only pin-money; it does not amount to a row of pins to the government. Why penalize them? If a woman earns $750, why place the man's income in a higher bracket? But that is exactly what happens. A man with a taxable income of $2,750 pays $218 this year and will pay $180 next year. If the wife works full time and earns $750, the net return is only $637. I cannot see any point in penalizing a woman who works like that with her hands. Hospitals are crying out for nurses, [Mr D. G. Ross.] 1
but married women are leaving the hospitals today because it is not worth their while to work in them.
Then, there are many women with nursing training who are married to doctors and others with fairly good incomes, but the fact that the wife is working, places the doctor in a 30, 40 or 50 per cent bracket. It is not worth while for the nurse to work under those conditions, and I should like to see something done about the matter. I make a plea to the government to raise the amount which married woman may be permitted to make, so that we may have their services. They would not be taking the place of other persons, or putting them out of employment. They would be going to places where others would not be going; and we need them more than we ever did. I plead with the government to do something about this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I was going to say a word. There has been a good deal of talk about this penalizing of married women, so far as the income tax schedules are concerned. But people overlook the fact that the exemption to married women is given on the assumption that the man is supporting his wife. If he is not supporting his wife, then the exemption should be either eliminated or curtailed, depending upon the circumstances.
In no other country in the world that I know of is the full married exemption given to a married man whose wife is also earning. In the United States they have the option of joining their incomes, and taking the full marriage exemption, which, of course, would be far less favourable than the provision we have in Canada.
And dividing by two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

No, not "dividing by two" -paying the tax on the joint income. They can divide the income and take single exemptions. And practically the same rule applies in Great Britain.
Our rule with respect to exemptions for married women is more favourable than that of any other country I have been able to find. Therefore I think the criticism of the treatment of married women, so far as the income tax law of Canada is concerned, is unjustified. And the combined effect of the reduction last year and this year means that the actual increased tax paid, with the wife earning in addition to her husband, who is in receipt of income, is extremely small.

However, they are not and we must have time for wage reports to come in and be checked in the office before deductions are made.
Would it not be possible for the minister to have the regulations changed so that these returns can be sent in by the 15th of the month instead of the 7th?
