speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I shall be very glad to look into it. I recognized that there is some cause for complaint in that district and in like districts with reference to sending in these returns.
That is perfectly true. I understand from the county clerk that this also was the condition in many townships, and no doubt the same is true of counties throughout the whole of Canada.

With reference to payroll deductions for income tax, has the minister or the government given any consideration to allowing a five per cent discount for wage-earners who have had the greater part of their income tax deducted from their pay by the end of the calendar year? The government has the use of this money for at least four months and the greater part of it for ten months, and at present no interest is allowed
to the wage-earners for the use of it. Businessmen and most professional men pay their income tax on the 30th day of April of the following year, so that they have the use of the money for four months after the close of the taxation year and no additional charge by way of interest is made against them for having had the use of this money for a period of at least four months. The wage-earner, who can often ill afford' to pay income tax at all, is therefore penalized for being prompt in his income tax payments through compulsory deductions, which begin with the first month of the taxation year. The government has the use of this money for many months, and so I think that when the wage-earner makes his final return in April he should be allowed to deduct at least five per cent from the income tax payable on that date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has referred to professional men, doctors, lawyers and the like. They have to make quarterly payments, in March, June, September and December, so that by the end of the year they have paid or should have paid their income tax in full. There is a provision in the act that, if they have underestimated, they have to pay interest on the amount of the underestimate. I do not think there is any substantial inequality of treatment between the wage-earner and the taxpayer who is required by the act to pay by quarterly instalments. It is not quite accurate to say that the government has had the use of the money during that period. The circumstance is simply this. The taxpayer is paying the proper proportion of the tax as he goes along. It is a strict pay-as-you-go policy, and the country gets the needed revenue from the earnings as they are paid out.

There is one obvious and unfair working of the income tax regulations which I should like to suggest to the government might be remedied in the present budget. This suggestion should, I think, meet with the support of all hon. members, and I believe it would apply personally to at least ninety-nine per cent of them. I refer in particular to the various sections of the act which allow an individual who comes under a retirement or pension plan set up by a company to deduct from his gross income before assessment the amount which he contributes under the plan.
Tomorrow we hope we may be on the old age pensions bill. We have seen that, even with the comparatively low income tax which we have had during the last thirty years or so, with the exception of the war years, the people of Canada to a substantial percentage

Income War Tax Act
have been unable to provide for their own old age, and that is why we have to give serious consideration to making some grants to ease their existence. Therefore, if our people, or a substantial number of them, have had difficulty in providing a competence for their old age under no personal income tax or a comparatively low rate we may imagine what our problem will be in the years to come when we are almost bound to have fairly substantial personal income taxes.
As I mentioned, if a worker comes under a company plan for retirement, which plan must be approved by the Minister of Finance, the company may make a contribution, perhaps four or five per cent or more of the wages which are paid the individual. A company is allowed a tax deduction for that amount. The worker is also allowed to make a contribution, which we will say is five per cent of his wages, to a plan leading to his retirement. This amount is also deductible from his income before tax assessment is made. Furthermore, the individual may, if he is just coming under a plan now and has been in the service of the organization or company for a number of years, make a deduction for the years of work which he has put in during which time he did not come under the plan, so that he has on two counts the possibility of making a deduction for his old age, and these deductions on the two counts are both subtracted from his gross income before the tax is calculated.
The great majority of Canadian people, however, are not fortunate enough to work for large companies or prosperous enough companies that have these retirement plans; therefore they do not have the same attractive and advantageous means of providing for I heir old age as this limited class of workers coming under the various plans. I shall read one section of the Income War Tax Act, so that members may perhaps more clearly understand the nature of these exemptions. I shall read from section 5, paragraph (g). These are deductions and exemptions allowed under the Income War Tax Act:
(i) An amount not exceeding nine hundred dollars in the taxation year, actually retained by the employer from the remuneration of the taxpayer for an employees' superannuation or pension fund or plan in respect of services rendered in the taxation year or paid by the taxpayer who is a member of a trade union as part of his union dues.
I am told that in negotiating contracts with their employers many trade unions insist that some retirement plan be put into effect before they sign with the company; so that it is clear that under the existing regulations there is a distinct, welcome and worthwhile advantage to the workers who come
under these plans. Altogether it can amount to a total of $900 under each of the three counts which I mentioned, which is $2,700 deducted from a man's income before tax. Of course a person would need to have an extraordinarily large income to be able to set aside that amount. But may I just point out in connection with these regulations which we now have under review that if no personal income tax were applied until the married man reached an income of $2,000 there would'be a saving of $70 a year in tax? If the man who at the present time does not come under a plan where able to come under such a plan, which I shall suggest later should be under government sponsorship, and put in his 870 which he now pays in tax, he would find that, starting at the age of thirty, when many a man wakes up to the fact that old age will eventually come upon him and that he had better start making some provision for it, and putting $70 a year into a dominion government annuity, he will at the age of seventy be able to receive an annuity of $700 a year; or if he prefers to retire at sixty-five, having paid until that age, he will be able to have an annuity of approximately $500 a year. It is obvious then that there is discrimination against the great majority of our people who are not fortunate enough to come under one of these company sponsored plans approved by the Minister of Finance.
The principle that is already contained in these plans is approved by the government but because of inertia or for some other reason, the government has not seen fit to devise a plan whereby these workers who do not come under the company plans may make some provision for their own old age.
I might say, in passing, that these amounts are not entirely free of tax. It is in a sense a delayed tax because, when the man retires and starts drawing his yearly amounts as annuity, if you like, under the plan, the whole amount that he receives is taxable year by year as he receives it. But this is fair to the government and also fair to the individual because, when the individual retires, he is not likely to have a substantial income and his tax on whatever he receives is likely to be moderate, just as exists under the plans now approved by the Minister of Finance.
At the present time, with the extraordinarily high tax rates that we have, it is almost impossible for a person, particularly in the lower brackets, to make adequate provision for himself or his wife or widow as the case may be. when he retires from work or dies. Taxation is already making too large an
Income H'ar Tax Act

inroad into our personal incomes to allow many a person to balance his budget, much less look forward to a day when he is not a regular wage-earner. Therefore anything that this committee can do to make it possible for a man to provide for his own old age should meet with the approval of every hon. member.
What I am suggesting is that the government under the Department of Labour, where the annuities branch now is, or under some other suitable department, frame an over-all plan containing the various provisions which the Minister of Finance now insists upon when he gives approval to a company-sponsored plan. That overfall plan under the government could be made open to all individuals who wish to pay into it in order to provide for their own old age. I am not suggesting at this moment that the government make a contribution to it, although the idea is capable of that elaboration, and perhaps further consideration should be given it. But if we look at it entirely from the angle of personal tax, there should be an opportunity for the individual, under the government plan, to do as much for himself as the government now allows him to do if he is fortunate enough to work for a company having such a plan.
It may be that our insurance companies, who act as trustee for many of these company-sponsored plans, might formulate an over-all plan which would allow individuals who are not employees of these favoured companies, as I shall call them, to come under a plan sponsored by individual insurance companies, and the ordinary citizen could take his choice of the plan of the dominion government or of the insurance company. I suggest this, not only because I am a supporter of private enterprise, but also because many people will no1! save or come under a plan like this, no matter how favourable it may be, or how much they may save in tax this year to provide for their eventual old age, unless the plan is sold to them; and it requires selling. It may be desirable, therefore, to have private institutions formulate government-approved plans, as well as the government itself.
I should hope that if the government does formulate, under the dominion government annuities, a plan such as I recommend, it will allow the same rate now allowed in respect of annuity accumulations, namely four*per cent, which is a somewhat higher rate than the artificially low rate at which the government is able to borrow at the present time. I would also suggest, because of the social nature of

this undertaking, that the government would, as in the case of government annuities, bear the cost of administration.
There would, be, of course, the usual provision which the minister now insists upon in the company plans in regard to a man on retirement not getting money out in a lump sum but spread over his life in the form of an annuity or some other form which would appeal to the minister. There would also be suitable provision made for the widow of a worker should he die and perhaps also for dependants in, case they are still young.
This is a proposal to allow people who are not able to participate in, the benefits now extended by the government under the company approved plans to look after, through the process of self-help, their own old age, so that they will not become dependent and so that they will have the feeling of self-reliance, which people cannot have if they must lean upon a paternal government.
What features does the hon. member's plan propose which are not included already in the group insurance annuity plan?

I do not know whether I understand entirely my hon. friend's question. I do not know exactly what he means by the group insurance annuity plan. He must be a little more specific. I suggest that unless a person comes under a company-sponsored plan, of which there are a great many, particularly during the last five years or so, when a greater feeling of social consciousness has swept across the country, he cannot possibly get the benefits which are extended to the individual who does come under such a plan.
Take our own situation in this house. I should think that not more than two or three per cent of the members would be eligible to come under these plans. The ordinary citizen cannot do it. The man in a large steel mill or in a coal company or some other industry that has a plan like this can get the benefit of it. As a guess, I should think not more than fifteen per cent of our working population, or perhaps I might make it twenty per cent, are eligible to take advantage of these plans, and many small employers do not feel that they can set up such a plan, having regard to the additional cost of the company contributions. If the government approves a plan there is also a contribution by the employer as well as by the employee. Some companies do not feel that they can accept the added responsibility, but what I am suggesting now is that the government set up a plan whereby the indi-

Income War Tax Act
vidual at least can do all that he could if he were working for a company maintaining a retirement plan.
Apparently there are no new benefits suggested in the hon. member's proposal.
I only want the benefit which the government has approved, so far as a particular section of the population is concerned, extended to the whole population.

I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosedale, and I would point out to the hon. member for Halifax the scope of the proposal. It would, in fact, cover all those people, or make it possible for all those people not engaged in industrial enterprise. under an employer or corporation who had set up superannuation benefits, to get the advantage of such a scheme. It would be an opportunity for the farmer, who has not a full-time employer, to contribute live per cent of his income to the dominion government on a superannuation basis, to be paid to him in instalments upon his attaining of a certain age, and without taxation, and that could be deducted from his income, after the manner of compulsory savings collected during the war.
I remember when compulsory savings were first introduced into this house, the then minister of finance did not feel that those who contributed to the superannuation plan under the Department of Labour should be entitled to consider their annual contribution to that as part of compulsory savings. After some consideration, the minister did yield to our exhortations that that should be allowed as part of compulsory savings.
In further answer to the hon. member for Halifax, I would ask the committee to realize that only a small percentage-my hon. friend says fifteen or twenty per cent-of our population work for employers who have set up a superannuation fund. I know many big firms who have never set up such a fund for their employees. I have in mind several in my own city who have had employees for twenty, thirty and forty years, and these people find themselves too old to continue working and without any superannuation set up for them. Consider the case of the independent-enterprise man, the small tradesman, the mechanic, the seasonally occupied man, the man who runs his own business or runs a small business for someone else. These people have not the advantage of a superannuation plan where the employer pays half and the individual half. Such a man has not even an opportunity of providing for his old age, getting a reduction from his income tax or assessable income for the purpose.
If we were to realize how this would work out, I think we would feel that it is, in effect, the most advantageous policy for old age pensions that we could have. So many people have said that we in Canada have reached the stage where we should have a contributory old age pensions scheme. This is a scheme that would replace that to a large extent, because any man who felt provident enough, beginning life at the age of twenty-one years of age, to provide five per cent of his income for dominion government annuity payment, deducting it as expense of living from assessable income, would at the age of sixty or sixty-five have sufficiently established a superannuation benefit to carry him along on a substantial income, so that he would be entirely independent of any gratuity from anybody. Our civil service has the advantage of the superannuation plan. Many people have argued that the civil servant gets compensation by virtue of the benefit he gets in being allowed to contribute to the superannuation fund and having the government contribute a like amount. The government need not contribute to the individual, but they could contribute by w'ay of administering the fund and by way of paying him in the same manner as is now adopted by the annuities branch of the Department of Labour, the amount being calculated mathematically on a four and a half per cent compound interest basis.
We all know that there is in existence in the Department of Labour a scheme under which individuals can make annual contributions until they are sixty, sixty-five or seventy years of age, and thus provide themselves, their wives and dependants with annuities ranging as high as $100 a month per person. That in itself is security against old age or mature age. If those who are not in industrial enterprise-and even those who are in industrial enterprise, if they want to take advantage of it-had an opportunity to contribute a small portion of their income each year, as part of their everyday living expense, and could have that exempted from income tax, they would become more self-sufficient and satisfied that they themselves were looking after their old age. They would not look to this government with anxiety for paternalistic legislation, as so many people would have us believe they do today.
I believe the fundamental spirit of our Canadian people is one of independence and thrift. I believe they want an opportunity to provide for themselves in their old age, and I believe the government should make that as easy as possible. I also believe that, in the long run, we would save a great deal
Income War Tax Act

of expense if that opportunity were given by way of annuity, if we were to give them the inducement so that they could set themselves up in that way with pride, independence and a feeling that they were getting at a later day something which they had provided for throughout their lives.
I highly commend the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosedale. Instead of thinking of a compulsory contribution to old age or retirement allowances, I believe the government would be well advised if they made it voluntary and gave the ordinary rank and file of our Canadian people who are in independent enterprise, assistance and cooperation. As the hon. member for Rosedale has said, I believe that this could be done through the annuities branch or through the insurance companies. I also believe that if this contribution were exempt from income tax, it should be made on the basis that it can be received back by the taxpayer only in annuity form in month to month payments and benefits at a time when he is most likely to need them. I believe the Minister of Finance would be well advised to take this matter into serious consideration, because I think the great mass of the Canadian people have not appreciated, or have not been encouraged to appreciate, the benefits of an annuity under the Department of Labour as it now stands; otherwise a great many more people would have taken out one, and we would not have the difficulty we have today, namely, that people feel they are about to face difficult days in the eve of their lives.

I should like to branch into another field with respect to income tax, and ask the minister a question which I fear is somewhat of a perennial one; perhaps it is perennial because of its importance. It is a question which arises from a series of inquiries received in the mails, and it must have come to the attention of hon. members on scores and scores of occasions. It concerns the person who has a self-contained domestic establishment, who has all the expenses, all the outlays and all the overhead that married people have, but who at the same time is not entitled to the same kind of consideration under the income tax law and regulations. It is a matter which, I think, touches the homes of many worthy and deserving people in Canada. I have listened to the arguments of those who have gone before, but I have not been convinced by them. After all, what is the use of our changing finance ministers unless we can expect something better from the new one than was received from the old one? On that basis I feel somewhat optimistic and not a little encouraged to press my 
case again for that group of people who, 1 think, are deserving and have been long-suffering and kind-perhaps too kind-to their government in the past for not having given them a little more consideration. I should like to ask the minister if he will, after I resume my seat, deal with that matter and give us the reasons he has finally designed which apparently have prevented the change.
The other matter to which I wish to refer is one which perhaps some people may consider small. But after all, as most public men will find, the small things in the world are really the big things. Certainly they are big things to the people we represent. Today we are experiencing the development of education in a way that we have never experienced before. Our seats of higher and secondary learning in every part of Canada are bulging with students; and I suppose that applies to every country of the world where education is available. In many cases one finds that the ordinary middle-class person is struggling to make ends meet. I do not make any apologies for saying a word on his behalf; and it is no reflection on those who are making less money, either; because, after all, that middle class of our people who are struggling hard to make ends meet, very often at the end of the year have just about the same amount left over as those in even lower brackets. In addition to that, in trying to educate their children they find that, after the boy or girl reaches the age of twenty-one, their exemption with respect to that child, as a dependent under the income tax law and regulations, ceases. They are then on their own without any of those considerations being available to them. I have had this matter brought to my attention within the last few months by several deserving citizens in my own constituency, and not all of them have been of my own political faith either. I should like the minister to give some consideration to cases of that type. As a nation we are now reaching the position where it is not so hard to see that if, in the years which lie ahead, education advances as much as it has in the past, we might conceivably find that university degrees in Canada are almost as numerous as senior matriculations were some twenty-five years ago. That, of course, makes a situation which, I think, deserves attention by the government because of conditions we see developing. I should like the minister to give some consideration to that class of people, who, I think, are worthy and deserving Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Dealing with the two points my hon. friend has raised, as he himself has indicated the first is not a new one, I

Income War Tax Act
think I have answered it myself on at least two previous occasions. That is the suggestion that a person who lives in a self-contained domestic establishment should be given the same treatment as a married man who lives in such an establishment, or a man who has such an establishment and maintains in it someone connected with him by blood relationship or marriage and who is wholly dependent upon him. Personally I have never considered that there was justification for extending that exemption to groups other than those already covered. After all, living in a self-contained domestic establishment, in a house, is a way of life. The exemption is given to a married man as part of his married exemption; and it is given to a widower or a single man who is maintaining in that type of establishment dependents who are connected with him in the degree mentioned in the act, as a further concession. But to give it to all taxpayers who choose to live in that way, I felt, and my predecessor also felt, was never justified, and personally I would not feel that we should extend the law at this time. I think I have given a similar answer on previous occasions.
The other question my hon. friend raised, namely the possibility of extending the exemption for children who are attending university when they get beyond the age of twen'ty-one, has been brought to my attention by a great many hon. members. I have had a number of letters concerning it, and it has been brought to my attention by several hon. members on this side of the house. There again the justification for allowing the exemption up to the age of twenty-one-and it is an exception to the general rule-is that this is about the age at which children complete or at any rate nearly complete their ordinary arts course. If they are going on to take professional training as a doctor or lawyer, or to do post-graduate work, that is usually after they have reached the age of twenty-one years. I am not quite sure just what income bracket my hon. friend means when he refers to "middle class", but I would think he meant someone receiving up to about $5,000 a year, would he?
I did not have in mind a figure that high. I think I used the words "middle class" where I meant the medium income class.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it is lower, so much
the better, because under the new rates on an income of up to $3,500 the top rate is twenty per cent, so that the value of the exemption to a taxpayer with an income of up to $3,500 would be only $60 a year. I will
concede that $60 a year is $60, and has some significance when you are sending a boy to college; but it is not a sum that is going to make the difference between sending him there and not sending him. I have never felt that we would really be justified in extending this exemption beyond the normal period within which a man is giving his boy or girl the initial university education.

Following that up, did I
understand the minister to say the exemption was given a widower with children in the same way as to a married man?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is true, if they are
wholly dependent upon him and under the age limit.
In a self-contained establishment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
But what about the widower himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The widower himself is the same as a bachelor. That is a way of life; he is living in a house instead of in an apartment or hotel or boarding house.

May I say one word to the minister with respect to my observations on the educational point? I did not have in mind people making as much as $5,000. In the one instance I have in mind I believe the man's income is just over $2,000, which I think, generally speaking, is not a large income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably he would not be paying any tax at all.	[DOT]

Well, his income may be over $2,000, bu't in any event it is in one of the lower income brackets. When I said "middle" perhaps I should have said one of the lower income brackets, because that is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To a man with an income of $5,000, the value of an exemption of $300 at the marginal rate would be $66 a year.
But take the person who is making something over $2,000, from $2,000 to $3,000. He has a pretty tough time trying to get his children educated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If he is a married man he gets an exemption of $1,500, and he would have an exemption of $100 for each child in receipt of family allowance and $300 for each child not in receipt of that allowance. My only point is that the value of the exemption is perhaps significant, but I should think it

Income War Tax Act
extremely unlikely that an individual with an income of $2,000 to $2,500 would be in a position, out of his own resources, to send his children to college. He could probably help them-
He does the best he can, and he should not have any obstacles placed in his way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course he does the best he can, but I think the children would have to help earn their way through college. The point is that he would get the exemption until his children were twenty-one, which is a very fair average age for completing an arts course at university, which covers a period of three to four years. If they are going on to post-graduate work, in the professions or otherwise, I do not think there should be an exemption which does not apply to other taxpayers.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Peel and the explanation of the minister on the first question raised, in regard to widowers, I should like to give the minister an example for his consideration. In this case in 1945 the widower had a pension of $624 and a small investment income which brought his total income to a little over $1,500. He is a widower maintaining his own home, with a housekeeper to whom he has to pay $40 a month. His taxes in 1945 amounted to $260. He is considered as a single person, even though he continues to maintain his home since the death of his wife. In 1946, on an income of $1,619, his tax amounted to $208.54. In that year, in order to help pay his way, his son had to contribute $300 out of his own income, and of course in turn the son had to pay income tax on his own income. This man is eighty-one years of age. By thrift and diligence he has made almost enough to maintain himself, but not quite; and I am asking the minister whether in a case of this kind, where a man is past the age of seventy years, we will say, some consideration should not be given him in respect of the exemptions, and whether the exemptions should not be increased from $750 to $1,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, consideration has
never been given, as far as I am aware, to increasing the exemptions solely by reason of the age of the taxpayer. I should think it would be undesirable from a good many points of view.

Then following the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's with respect to the exemptions of married women earning
salaries, my opinion has been that v/e should
protect the exemption of $750 given a married woman, and maintain it as it was in 1946. I see the minister is not sympathetic to that point of view, because, as I understood him a few moments ago, he said he did not favour a special dispensation to any class in order to induce people to work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say "dispensation." I said I was not in favour of income tax concessions to any group in order to persuade them to work.

This year, 1947, we have certain problems to meet, and probably the most important of- them is the question of production. Engaged in business as I am, it seems to me that the minister has lost sight of the fact that if we do not protect the exemption which was given to nurses, teachers and stenographers in 1946 we are going to lose these women from industry, As a matter of fact, I was interested in the table the minister filed, and I shall certainly be interested in perusing it, when I have a chance to do so, because in my attempts to find out what the tax on married women earning incomes in Canada amounted to, from questions which I asked of the Minister of National Revenue, I discovered that there had not been any statistics kept in respect of the tax paid by those married women in the years up to this date, although the situation will probably be changed from now on.
But I did get an estimate from a departmental official as to what the situation really was, and this is it. The total salaries and wages earned by women in Canada in 1946 is estimated at about $607,000,000. This does not include income from investments. It is estimated that twenty-five per cent of the women in business are married women, and seventy-five per cent are single. That is only an estimate. Therefore $148,000,000 represents the income earned by married women in 1946. For the most part these earnings were in the low-income group.
It is estimated that the number of married women who earned this amount of wages and salaries was 110,000, so that the average annual wage or salary per person was $1,350. It is estimated that the tax upon salaries and wages of married women paid in 1946 amounted to $18,000,000.
There is nothing very scientific about that return because, as a matter of fact, it is only an estimate, and apparently it is not taken from any statistics at all. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare will probably have something to say a little later on when he finds there are not enough nurses

in the country to take care of the work to be done in the hospitals, if eventually we have a national health insurance plan.
I think the minister might very well give consideration to this matter of protecting the 1946 exemption for married women. I do not like to let his statement go unchallenged that he does not intend to give any special concession to any class in order to induce people to work, because, after all, production is the thing we are looking for this year. speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in support of the two points made by the hon. member for Peel. In a sentence or two, may I say my interest in this matter stems, in particular, from a number of widowers living in Weston, a part of Winnipeg. These are men who are employees in the shops of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, who have small homes. But even though they are widowers, they endeavour to keep those homes together as a place for the children to come, whether they be married or single. I rose not only to support the suggestions made by the hon. member for Peel, but to encourage him to carry on. And the means I shall use to encourage him is to make reference to something I now hold in my hand. As some hon. members may recall, in every budget debate since I came to this house-
That is not long ago.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
-I have spoken as strongly as I can with reference to a discrimination between railway train conductors and railway sleeping-car conductors. The minister will probably remember some of the discussion he and I have had across this floor. I had some discussions with his predecessor, and some with the present Secretary of State, who was then minister of national revenue.
I was told every year that it simply could not be done, and that, because of the distinction in the manner in which the incomes were received by these different employees, a line had to be drawn. The railway train conductors, being on a mileage basis, were allowed their away-from-home expenses as a taxation deduction; but the sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters, because they worked for wages or salaries, were not allowed their away-from-home expenses.
It would make interesting reading if I were to quote from Hansard the arguments used by the ministers I have mentioned when they 83166-227
told me that it simply could not be done. I am happy to say I hold in my hand a directive from the deputy minister, signed by F. H. Brown, deputy minister of taxation. This is directive No. 14. dated May 2, 1947, and the subject matter is the assessment of railway men's away-from-home expenses. It states:
The same consideration will be given to claims for away-from-home expenses of those railway men who are paid on a salary or wage basis as is given to those paid on a mileage basis.
I wish to express my thanks to the government for having acceded to this request. It did not come from me in the first place, although I have been fighting for it here. It came to the department from the unions and brotherhoods representing the men. I am sure it is clear now that it was a discrimination which should not have been maintained for such a long time.
Speaking particularly for the sleeping-car conductors and sleeping-car porters, and also for those other railway employees who are on a wage or salary basis, may I say that they appreciate the fact that they now have the same right as these other railway employees, namely that of charging their away-from-home expenses as part of the cost of their job.
So I say to the hon. member for Peel that probably his arguments are not in vain.
How many times did the hon. member have to present them?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I have presented mine for only three; I have only one year to go.
Mr. KNOWLES; The Minister of Labour will note that I said a minute ago that I did not start the suggestion. It came from the brotherhoods and the unions representing the men. However I did say that I led the fight on the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise to take part in this discussion in order to say something which may seem to be in an entirely different vein from the views I have just expressed. What I shall say grows out of a statement made to me in Winnipeg two or three nights before I left home last January to come to Ottawa to attend this session of parliament.
The man who spoke to me was a carpenter named Gus Johnson, a gentleman I have known for some time. He was giving me a bit of advice about the session, and made this interesting suggestion: "Don't worry too much about trying to get taxes reduced, but give the government so-and-so for their failure to give us good value for our taxes".

Income War Tax Act

I think it is really regrettable that the unfairnesses and injustices in the taxation structure, about which we have been talking during the course of this debate, lead us to a point where sometimes we consider that our main job is to try to have taxes reduced. I think the far more important thing is to find out what the government does with the tax moneys. I would say to the government of the day that their future depends not so much upon the taxation structure as upon the measures they take to achieve a really high level of economic activity, to raise the level of wages and the standard of income of all our people and to provide definite social security. It has been said a good many times in this debate, but it is well to repeat it, that one of the most striking remarks made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech was his admission that more than half of the income earning people in Canada receive incomes below the income tax exemption level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am quite prepared to abbreviate my remarks. I have made my point that the important thing is what the government does with the taxes it collects.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

There is a matter to which I would direct the attention of the minister in the hope that something will be done. This is the second time that I have referred to it.
I referred to it about ten months ago. It has to do with the income tax on domestic servants, particularly those in the maritime provinces.
In order to arrive at the income of a domestic servant for taxation purposes under the Income War Tax Act, the value of board and lodging provided- by the employer is added to the wages the servant receives. When a domestic servant in the maritime provinces files an income tax return he or she is obliged to add to the cash received as wages the sum of $26 a month or $312 a year for 'board and lodging supplied by his or her employer; but when a domestic servant in the province of Quebec files his or her income tax return he or she is required to add to the cash income received, not $26 a month or $312 a year for board and lodging, bult $15 a month or $180 -a year. It is ridiculous to suggest that a domestic servant employed in the maritime provinces has board and lodging any better or at greater cost than a domestic servant who is living in a mansion in Montreal or vicinity, or in some luxurious apartment house in Montreal, or in any other city in the province of Quebec. These hard-working people who reside in the mari times are being discriminated against. They are, in my opinion, getting an unfair deal. There is no reason why their income should be increased in this unfair manner and their taxes increased in consequence. Last year, on July 24, I brought this matter to the attention of the present Minister of Finance, -and I was supported in the stand I took by the hon. member for Halifax who said that he also had received complaints. The present minister said then that he would be glad to look into the matter and he added:
I agree with both members that there should be no discrimination between servants employed in the maritimes and those employed in other provinces. I shall look into the matter and see what is causing this condition.
I do not know whether the minister in 'the past ten months has had an opportunity to look into the matter or not, but I am informed that this discrimination continues. It

should have been done away with long ago. In fact it should never have existed. I would ask the minister why this discrimination exists. I have given the amounts that are imposed on domestic servants in the mari-times and in Quebec for board and lodging. I have referred to Quebec, because that is the only other province for which I have the figures. I ask the minister to give us the figures that are imposed for board and lodging in the other provinces.
While I am on my feet, I should like to direct the minister's attention to another matter that was brought up last year by the hon. member for Halifax when he supported me on the taxation of domestic servants. At that time he said that he had brought to the minister's attention, then the acting minister of finance, the case of railway porters, stewards and waiters who operate on the Atlantic division between Halifax and Montreal. I do not know whether that situation has been remedied or not, but it does seem to me unfair that that condition should have existed. I would ask the minister if that situation has been remedied and, if not, why it has not been.

Before the minister replies, may I say briefly that I support what has been said by the hon. member for St. John-Albert. I very well recall bringing before the minister last July the case of the porters, stewards and waiters of the Canadian National railway system in particular. So far as I know, that situation still exists in the Atlantic region and does not apply either to the central or western divisions of the Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Answering, both hon. gentlemen who have just spoken, following the statements which were made last year I took the matter up with the then deputy minister, Mr. Elliott, and was told at the time that there was no discrimination. My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, will look into the matter at once. I dloubt whether there is any discrimination. another. When I get the answer I should like to have the information I asked for in regard to the other provinces. I said I referred only to Quebec because these were the only figures I had. The information I gave referred to the city of Montreal, which showed that it was $15 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will get the full statement.
It was $15 a month for board and lodging, w'hile it was $26 a month in New Brunswick and other parts of the maritimes. I should like to have the figures for the other provinces as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will give my hon. friend a full statement as to what is allowed in all the provinces. It may require consultation- I do not know; I am not the Minister of National Revenue-with inspectors in the various districts. But my hon. friend is entitled to the information which he has asked for, and I know that my colleague will see that he gets it.

May I return the discussion for a moment to the subject brought up by the hon. member for St. Paul's and the hon. member for Parkdale, namely, the meagre exemption of $250 allowed as an income tax deduction for employed married women?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know my hon. friend wants to be accurate. A married woman pays no tax until she earns over $750 a year. But if she earns over $250 her husband's exemption is decreased proportionately.

I thank the minister for checking me up on that. That was the point I wanted to make. There are many husbands whose wives are employed to some extent or partly employed, making up to $250 or between $250 and $700 a year. The husbands of these women are called upon to inform their employers of their wives' income so that the proper deduction can be made from their pay. It may be a small point but I think it' is fairly important, in that there are many men who do not care to inform their employers that their wives are working. For that reason it leads to a number of women giving up their jobs, a number of women who are in essential employment, and I shall refer to only one
Income War Tax Act

case, namely, that of laundries. I do not suppose there is an hon. member in the committee who, during the last year, has not had some difficulty in having his laundry returned to him. If they have not, 1 am sure that the wives know of the situation which exists today all across Canada with regard to laundries and that type of business which employs a high percentage of women. Laundries have been hit particularly hard by this tax ruling, as have restaurants, bakeries and other types of business employing women workers chiefly. You have only to walk down the street of any big city today to see the signs in the windows saying "waitress wanted" to know what is happening in the country. If one wishes to get an impressive illustration of the situation today he has only to refer to the want ad sections of the daily newspapers. I realize that this employment problem is bringing a large revenue to the daily papers, and I would be the last one to want to cut into their revenue, but you see column after column of advertising asking for women to take employment in all types of industry. I am one who feels strongly that this ruling which says that income tax must be paid by the husband on the amount between $250 and $750 on his wife's wages, has caused this situation to a great extent.

I have two examples of what appears to me to be discrimination so far as income tax payments are concerned. I had a communication from the widow of a doctor who lived in my part of the city. When the doctor died some three years ago he left not only his wife but two daughters. In the meantime both the daughters have married and moved out of the city. One moved to Hamilton, but I do not know to what place the other moved. It is necessary for this lady to retain the services of her servant or maid, and she has complained to me in the strongest language that it is impossible for her to carry on. She has lived in the home for thirty years and raised her family there. While that is only one example, there are many other such cases. I should like to know if the government has in view any amendment or regulation to give redress to cases such as that.
Earlier in the evening some hon. member mentioned widowers. I know of many widowers who retain their own homes. A few moments ago the minister said, well, if they cannot keep their home they can go to a boarding house or apartment, or something to that effect. That does not seem to me to be fair treatment to a widower who wants to keep up his home so that his family may come to stay with him or visit him for the
holiday or longer in the summer time. Has the department additional allowance in view along that line?
Let me give another case which does not seem fair. Take a man in a position like the Prime Minister of this country. I have no right perhaps to mention his case, but he occupies a big home like many other men who keep up big homes. However, in the case of the Prime Minister he is under a tremendous expense because he must keep a home to receive and perhaps to take care of those who may visit him. In his case he is forced to pay heavy taxation and has little allowance, being a bachelor. There seems to be an acute need for improvement in our income tax set-up. The two examples I have mentioned do not seem to be quite fair. What is the real explanation of the treatment meted out to the widow or widower and to bachelors maintaining homes such as the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the exemption is based on married status or its equivalent. In the case of the widow to whom he has referred, when her husband died and she was supporting the two children in the house she had a $1,500 exemption. If her children marry and go away that exemption is reduced to that of a single person, $750, and if she is in the income tax bracket that I was discussing a .moment ago with the hon. member for Peel she would pay something in the order of $100 to $150 a year more tax than she did before her husband died or while she was still supporting children in the house. But that applies to everyone who lives in a house. It is a way of life, and we do not assist in paying for self-contained domestic establishments by giving increased exemptions if the taxpayer has no dependents to support.
As regards the bachelor, I do not know that we should amend the income tax law to allow the Prime Minister to get an additional income tax credit. These are the reasons. The additional exemption is due to the married status or its equivalent. It is not an inducement, but a special concession handed out to those who are supporting wives and children or dependents.

I wish to join with
those who have spoken in disapproval of the income tax as a means of discouraging people from working. The minister expresses unwillingness to modify the income tax in such a way as to encourage people to work. I suggest to him that the country wants him to say whether or not he is equally unwilling to modify the income tax structure so as to discourage people from working. The

Income War Tax Act
Canadian people, generally speaking, need no encouragement to work if they are given the chance, but it is certainly unfair to discourage them from working, and I maintain that for the last several years the income tax structure has been such as to discourage them from doing work that needs to be done. The time has come to overhaul the income tax structure in order to see that such defects in it are corrected.
I wish to say one thing more and it has to do with production on the farms. I do not know whether it has been brought to the minister's attention, but if it has not I should like to point it out to him now. There is a serious falling off of production in western Canada, at least in the matter of hogs, beef, wool and a great many other things which are needed vitally in the life of the nation. This situation is bad and should be remedied. A few days ago I had a letter from an outstanding agriculturist in my constituency, who, speaking of hogs, said that the falling off in production was not the result particularly of the price of grain or the scarcity of grain or the scarcity of labour or the price of hogs, but simply of the fact that if a man came in after a hard day's work feeding hogs to produce food for the nation he was immediately penalized for doing so. Surely no intelligent group of people governing a nation will permit such a condition to continue. I hope that is sufficiently emphatic and does not need to be remarked upon again.
I would say this in conclusion. I think the suggestion this man made to me in his letter was sound. He said that the first $800 which a man makes from producing, on the side, food such as beef, pork, eggs, butter, potatoes and other needs of life ought to be exempt from taxation, regardless of what his taxation might be in respect of other activities on his farm. That may present some difficulties, but these difficulties must be met and overcome, because this tendency to discourage production of food in this country must be stopped.

The Iron, member for Winnipeg North Centre tells me he did not finish his story in connection with Gus Johnson, his Swedish friend. Gus mentioned that he did not like the income tax particularly, but ten years ago he was on relief, and he is much happier paying income tax on an income than he would be back on relief. I think he was speaking for the great majority of Canadians. We do not like income tax very well, but most of us would rather have an income that places us in the income tax brackets than belong to the majority of Canadian wage-earners who do not receive an income high enough to be taxable. I will not pursue that line further.
Members of this group have repeatedly emphasized the fact, that it is not the amount of income tax one pays that is important but rather the amount one has left after paying the tax. Ministers of finance have never been able to satisfy the members of our group but we persevere in our argument. It was the minister of finance of New Zealand. Hon. Walter Nash, who captivated the minds of members of our parliament when he was here early in the war, when he outlined the fiscal policy of his country. He said that no one who put on a uniform for hie country should find himself in a worse position because of his service, and, second, that no one who remained at home should find himself in a better position because of having remained at home.
I thought that these opinions had been forgotten by members of the Canadian cabinet, but I happened to be in Montreal in January of this year and heard the Minister of National Defence speak at a public gathering, when he said that it was the policy of the Canadian government so to prosecute the war that, no one who put on a uniform for his country would be in a worse position because of having offered his service, and he mentioned the fact that the Minister of Veterans Affairs was doing everything in his power to see that those who served Canada in the army, air force and navy would not be in a worse position than if they had remained at home. The Minister of National Defence was given a warm ovation when he mentioned that his colleague from Montreal, St. Antoine-Westmount, the present Minister of Finance, was doing his job in seeing that those who remained at home were not to be in a better position financially because of having remained at home.
I am afraid, however, the record of performance will not support that claim. Recently the Minister of National Revenue tabled some information in reply to some of my questions. The information was given on May 26, indicating the financial position of our people in the top brackets. The minister did not reveal how many Canadians receive incomes of $200,000 or more. The Minister of Agriculture gave approximate information. Apparently he has information that is not available to the rest of us. He indicated that there are between twenty and twenty-five in that bracket and suggested it was not really worth while for the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar to raise this question.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that it would make a difference of roughly $200 million.

I hope the fact that the Minister of Finance made no reference to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosedale, and supported by the hon. member for Carleton, does not mean that he was not interested in it. Indeed I very much hope that he may say something about it. To me it seemed to be a most important and interesting suggestion, and I would think it has to do with something which, regardless of party, we in this house would approve, namely, helping people to help themselves. I appreciate that there may be difficulties. The difficulties of administration may be great. I understand that it is
one thing to have a pension plan brought forward by an organization which can take care of all the details, which can practically assure the minister that the thing will be carried out in a businesslike way, and that it is another thing to deal with individuals. Nevertheless, it seems to me that there is basically an inescapable fairness in what the hon. member for Rosedale suggested. Once more may I say that it seems to me that, to whatever extent it may be made effective, the suggestion does move in the direction in which, as I said a moment ago, I believe we all want to go, namely, helping people to help themselves. Therefore I would earnestly hope that the minister would find it in his heart to say that the idea is of interest, that it will not be disregarded, that, in spite of the difficulties, the thing will be studied and whatever else he feels he can say with regard to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I was greatly interested in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosedale, and I intend to study carefully what he said. Of course, offhand I can see certain obvious objections. Any such government plan which was made purely voluntary would mean that some people would come in to it and some would not. I agree that it is desirable to get people to help themselves as much as possible; but if you have a government plan of that kind which is purely voluntary, you will be faced with some people who have provided their own social security and others who have been improvident and have not done so, but who, nevertheless, if in need, will insist upon being looked after and who will have to be looked after in their old age. So that offhand it would seem to me that is one objection. However, the subject is one which has a great many ramifications and would require a great deal of study. I was most interested in what the hon. gentleman said, and he can rest assured, as can the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, that I will study it carefully. Other than that, I cannot be expected to offer any comment this evening.

I should like to mention two problems which were laid before me by the representatives of the halibut fleet in Prince Rupert. For the people in many of the fishing villages up the British Columbia coast the cost is quite heavy when they go to a hospital, especially if they have to take their families along with them for medical purposes. They wish to have the cost of transportation to a hospital included in the amount which is deductible for medical expenses. It is getting prohibitive for a man, his wife and

Income TVar Tax Act
family to live in these villages up the coast if medical attention is needed for the family. They cannot afford to go out to get it. I also found out that, owing to the fact that there is a shortage of accommodation in the hospitals at the present time, these people who come from Massett in the Queen Charlotte islands and go down to Vancouver to receive hospitalization are told that they must leave the hospital as soon as possible. Granted that while they are in hospital, the amount of their expense is deductible; but when they are discharged from hospital and have to live in Vancouver in order to receive treatment in the hospital each day, the cost of their board and room and their expenses while living in Vancouver is something they are not able to put in as a deduction. Further, if they get drugs through any other source than the hospital, they are not able to mark up their cost as a deduction. Therefore, on behalf of the small communities on the coast, especially where the fishermen live, in order that these communities may grow and become prosperous, I should like to have the benefits I have mentioned extended to these people.
Another matter is one which I can best outline by reference to a letter sent by the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Settlement Service to the inspector of income tax in Vancouver. It reads in part:
In many instances we have cases where assessments are not made for three years after the return is filed, and any differences there may be are assessed and on this non-payment interest is charged for the full three years, and both the fishermen and myself feel that this is not fair and interest should be charged from the date of assessment.
In some cases the mistake may be made by the income tax office itself; yet the fishermen has to pay the interest on the amount he owes, even though it is not his mistake. Some rectification should be made in regard to this matter, because it has been a burning problem there, as many of the men have had interest charged against them where really it should not have been charged.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will take note of my hon. friend's remarks and see what, if anything, can be done.

I wish to refer to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for St. John-Albert. The minister stated that he would produce the figures for the various provinces as to the amounts which domestic servants are required to show in their income tax returns for board and lodging. I wonder if he would do the same thing as far as hired men in the various provinces are concerned.
I have heard a few' complaints in regard to the matter, and I think it might be well perhaps to have it cleared up at the same time.
I have reference to hired men on farms. I do not know whether it is practical or not to do anything about the matter but in our part of the country at any rate the fact that the farmer has been required to collect the income tax out of the payment he makes to his hired man has been productive of a great deal of difficulty and a great deal of trouble. The practical effect of this requirement has been that the farmer who himself turned in an income tax return and in that return reported what he paid to his hired man and deducted from his hired man's wages the amount required, in most cases lost his hired man and lost him to the man who did not turn in an income tax return or who turned in an incorrect one, we will say, or something along that line. As I say, I do not know whether there is any practical means of correcting that situation, but I should like to bring it to the minister's attention, because it has been the reason why at least two farmers whom I know have had to cease business in our part of the country, owing to the fact that they could not get hired men. Their hired man said, "Well, you are taking so much a month away from me because of income tax. Nobody else around the country is doing it, and I won't work here". These people found it impossible to keep hired men, so they just quit. They were oldish people anyway, and could not carry on by themselves.
As I say, the average farmer is not in the same class as the businessman wTho keeps regular books and is in a position to make deductions from the wages he pays his employees. A large number of farmers do not know anything about this and just will not bother with it. As a result, I say it works out in a very unfair way to the people who do make an effort to comply with the law. and causes them to lose their hired men. It seems to me that, from the practical point of view, the amount of money the government would realize through collections made in its behalf by farmers from hired men would not be sufficient to compensate for the difficulty and trouble it causes, so I would ask that the matter be given some thought and consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that.

I should like to get same information from the minister. Once before I thought we had this matter settled, but I see the administration entirely ignores some of the answers given by the former minister, so I vould like to have this thing squared up and
Income War Tax Act

perhaps get some definite information so that farmers making up their tax returns may know exactly where they stand. This form I hold in my hand is the blue form used by farmers. On the back, under the heading, "Notes re farm receipts and expenses", I find this paragraph:
4. Produce used from "family garden" and small sums usually termed "pin money" obtained by the wife, sons or daughters, by their own efforts, need not be taken into account.
I understand that the practice, at least in the Edmonton district, is that all this has to be accounted for, even though in most cases produce of this kind is raised by the wife and children. They are allowed no wages whatever for the work they do, and the farmer is billed for income tax on all the income received from the sale of all produce, whether raised by himself, his hired help, or his wife and family. Then again under the same heading I see this paragraph:
Produce raised on the farm and consumed in the farm home:	Include only commercial produce raised for sale as part of regular farm operations. Do not include produce of unsaleable quality or produce from family garden. Value at price you would ordinarily receive for the produce.
I understand that in the Edmonton district a charge of $50 is made against each member of the family for produce grown and consumed on the farm. I should like some definite information in connection with this clause, which, I understand, has been causing a great deal of trouble, because there is not uniformity of administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, I shall have that looked into. It will not be possible to give an answer tonight, but I will try to give it on the. section of the bill relating to the income tax schedules.

I would be glad if the minister would do that.
Then, before getting away from some other points that have been raised, I should like to ask the minister some questions in connection with the brief presented not so long ago by the Alberta Farmers' Union and the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section. On May 12, when I was speaking on the budget, I did not have sufficient time to complete what I wanted to say, so I am going to bring these points to the attention of the minister now so that he may give me the answers at the same time.
These organizations are asking for a four-year average for income tax purposes, for farmers. I realize that we now have a three-year average, but I believe that should be extended to four or even five years in order 
to give a fair average. Then they recommend that in the case of dispersal sales of live stock, an equivalent number of animals to those owned on January 1, 1941, be considered a capital asset and not subject to income tax. I believe there is just cause for complaint in this connection, and I should like very much to have the minister give, this matter consideration also.
Next they ask that the exemptions be increased to $1,200 and $2,400 for single and married persons respectively. The minister has told us there will not be any changes in the exemptions this year, but I am going at least to request that further consideration be given this point.
The next request is that an allowance be made for the labour of farm families in connection with production on the farms. For many years those of us who represent agricultural constituencies have been trying to get some allowance or some exemption from income tax on account of the work done by farm wives and families. Up to the present time we have not been successful, but I am hoping that at last the government will see that some justice is done ini this connection.
Then, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary East, these organizations request that the farmer should not be made responsible for income tax deductions from the wages of his hired help. As the hon. member has said, farm help is scarce; if a farmer collects the tax on the wages of his hired man, that man will just go to the farmer next door and get a job there, and the first farmer will be left without heip.
Then they recommend that payments of arrears of principal on the farm home, and on machinery debts and all that kind of thing, contracted prior to 1940 when we were coming out of the depression, should be allowed as an expense of the year in which the payments are made.
They also request that the income tax form be simplified. If all the farmers were bookkeepers they would be able to get along with the present forms, but since they are not bookkeepers it is quite a job for them to make out these returns.
Then item No. 12 in this brief requests uniformity of interpretation and administration of the act, and I believe that request should be given consideration.
Another question which has caused some trouble is in regard to the expense incurred by farmers in brushing and breaking land. I find that in some cases a farmer who has hired an outside man, perhaps a contractor, to clear and break his land is not allowed that expense as a deduction. In one instance which I referred to the department, they did allow

Income War Tax Act
the cost of breaking, because that was ploughing, but not the cost of brushing; but before this particular piece of land could lie ploughed, it had to be brushed. I believe that should be taken into consideration as an expense and allowable in the year in which payment is made. If the farmer hires a man by the month or by the year and has him do that work, there is no question whatever about the expense being allowed as a deduction.
Then I believe money expended in drilling or boring wells or excavating dugouts on the farm, together with all equipment for this work, should be chargeable as a current expense. That has not been done in the past; only recently, I think, have farmers claimed depreciation on wells and other things of that kind. I believe consideration should be given this request also.
Then I am going to give the minister a suggestion that was made by one of my constituents in Hughenden, a man named Nicholson, who discussed the income tax with me last fall. He suggested that the government include in its programme of public information some information dealing with the making up of income tax returns by farmers. If the government does not find it feasible to do this by way of radio programmes I would suggest that a booklet be made up setting out the things allowable as expenses and giving all other information, so that farmers may understand exactly what the department expects of them in connection with filing their returns.
